items.title: Data and frequency
items.content: Organise observations in a frequency table; total frequency \(N=\sum f\). Range \(=\) maximum − minimum.

items.title: Central tendency
items.content: Ungrouped mean \(=\sum x/n\); frequency mean \(=\sum fx/\sum f\). Median is the middle ordered value (or mean of two middle values). Mode is the most frequent value.

items.title: Graphs
items.content: Read axis labels and scales carefully. Bar charts compare categories; line graphs show change; histograms display continuous grouped data with touching bars.

items.title: Exam checks
items.content:
Check that frequency totals match the number of observations.
Averages describe centre; range describes a simple measure of spread.

items.title: Grouped frequency mean
items.content: For class intervals, use each class midpoint (x) as a representative value: approximate mean (= rac{sum fx}{sum f}). A midpoint is ((	ext{lower limit}+	ext{upper limit})/2).

items.title: Tables and frequency
items.content: Worked example: values 1, 2, 3 occur 2, 4, 1 times. Total frequency is 7 and sum is \(1(2)+2(4)+3(1)=13\).

items.title: Mean from raw data or frequencies
items.content: Worked example: data 3, 5, 5, 7 have mean \(20/4=5\). From a frequency table use \(\sum fx/\sum f\).

items.title: Median
items.content: Order data first. Worked example: 2, 4, 7, 9, 12 has median 7; for 2, 4, 7, 9, the median is \((4+7)/2=5.5\).

items.title: Mode and multimodal data
items.content: The mode is the most frequent observation. Worked example: 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3 has mode 3. A data set can have more than one mode or no repeated value.

items.title: Range and spread
items.content: Worked example: for 4, 11, 13, 18, range is \(18-4=14\). Range uses only extremes.

items.title: Grouped data and graph reading
items.content: For grouped continuous data, class intervals must not overlap; read bar height/scale and units before comparing values. Worked example: a bar reaches 6 divisions on a scale of 5 students per division, so its frequency is 30 students.

items.title: Class intervals and midpoints
items.content: A grouped table collects values into non-overlapping intervals. Use each midpoint as a representative value when estimating a grouped mean. Worked example: interval 10–20 has midpoint 15; with frequency 4 it contributes (4(15)=60) to (sum fx).

items.title: Find a mean
items.content: Worked example: 6, 8, 10, 12 have mean \(36/4=9\).

items.title: Find a median
items.content: Sort first, then locate middle position(s). Worked example: 3, 4, 8, 10, 15, 20 gives median \((8+10)/2=9\).

items.title: Find a frequency mean
items.content: Worked example: values 2 and 5 have frequencies 3 and 2. Mean is \( (2\cdot3+5\cdot2)/5=16/5=3.2\).

items.title: Compare distributions
items.content: Use mean/median for centre and range for simple spread; inspect units and possible outliers. Worked example: for 2, 3, 4, 5, 20 the mean is 6.8 but median is 4; the outlier pulls the mean upward.

items.title: Interpret a graph or table
items.content: State the category, value, and unit. Compare changes using the labelled scale rather than visual height alone. Worked example: a rise from 40 to 55 students is an increase of 15 students; the percentage increase is 15/40 × 100 = 37.5%.

items.title: Estimate a mean from grouped data
items.content: Find each class midpoint, multiply by its frequency, sum the products, then divide by total frequency. Worked example: classes 0–10 and 10–20 with frequencies 2 and 3 have midpoints 5 and 15; estimated mean (=(2·5+3·15)/5=11).

items.title: Why the frequency mean is weighted
items.content: A value \(x\) occurring \(f\) times contributes \(fx\) to the total. Summing gives \(\sum fx\); divide by total observations \(\sum f\).

items.title: Why median resists extreme values
items.content: The median depends on middle rank(s), not the magnitude of the largest or smallest observation. This makes it less affected by an outlier than the mean.

items.title: Why range measures spread
items.content: The largest and smallest values span the observed data interval; their difference gives its width, though it ignores interior variation.

items.title: Derive the grouped mean estimate
items.content: Replace each observation in a class by that class midpoint (x). The estimated total is (sum fx); dividing by the total count (sum f) gives the estimated mean. It is an estimate because original values within each interval are not known.

sections.title: Common errors and how to avoid them

items.title: Finding median before sorting
items.content: Always arrange values in ascending order first.

items.title: Wrong denominator for frequency mean
items.content: Divide by total frequency, not number of distinct values.

items.title: Reading graph scale incorrectly
items.content: Check each tick interval, axis origin, labels, and units.

items.title: Calling any repeated value the mode
items.content: The mode must have the greatest frequency; ties can produce multiple modes.

items.title: Using a class boundary instead of its midpoint
items.content: For a grouped mean estimate, multiply each class frequency by the class midpoint, not only the lower or upper boundary.

keyTakeaways: Median is based on ordered position.
